newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia sending troops back to demilitarized zone.
newsitem.headline: Colombia sending troops back to demilitarized zone.

text.p: The army prepared on Monday to pour 5,000 troops back into southern Colombia after being forced to cede a huge zone temporarily to leftist guerrillas.

Troops pulled out of a 5,000-square-mile (13,000-sq.-km) swathe of Caqueta province 32 days ago to permit Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) guerrillas to free 70 troops, some of whom they had held prisoner for more than nine months.

"I will restart operations (from midnight on Monday) to consolidate (control) of the area that we won back from the narco-subversives at great cost," Gen. Agustin Ardila of the army's 4th Division told Reuters. "This is not going to be a D-Day-style landing. ... I'm under no pressure of time."

In a successful effort to resolve Latin America's longest-running hostage crisis, President Ernesto Samper ordered the army to withdraw from the area in late May. The rebels then released their captives in a public ceremony attended by government representatives and foreign diplomats in the central square of Cartagena del Chaira, the main town in the demilitarized zone, on June 15.

The event was another humiliating blow to the army. The 60 soldiers were captured in an attack on the Las Delicias military base in neighbouring Putumayo province last Aug. 30 -- one of the worst defeats suffered by the military in Colombia's three-decade-old internal conflict.
The 10 marines were captured in a separate firefight in the northwestern province of Choco in January.
Ardila said he would be deploying an elite unit of special forces along with counterinsurgency troops backed by a small fleet of helicopter gunships and navy river boats.

He said civilians were helping provide vital intelligence information because they were anxious to see the "clowns of narco-subversion" driven out of the area. The phrase echoed a comment by Gen. Harold Bedoya, the armed forces chief, that the handover had been a "circus attended by many clowns."
Many local inhabitants told Reuters last week they feared the army would take revenge on them on suspicion that they had collaborated with the FARC.

Anti-drug police are also due to restart spraying illicit drug plantations in the region on Tuesday. Coca -- the raw material for cocaine production -- is a mainstay of the peasant economy there. The authorities accuse the FARC of controlling drug trafficking routes in and out of the region.
